questions.stimulusText:
Maya had promised to help her grandfather sort the contents of his workshop before the new shelves arrived. Most objects were easy to classify: screws went into jars, sandpaper into a drawer, and rulers into a wooden bin. Then she found a small brass bell wrapped in newspaper.
“That belonged above the door of my first bicycle shop,” Grandfather said. He tapped it, but the bell produced only a dull click.
Maya examined the clapper and discovered that a thin wire had bent against the side. She reached for pliers, then stopped. “If I straighten it too quickly, it might snap.”
Her grandfather nodded and returned to labeling boxes. Maya loosened the wire a little at a time, testing the bell after each adjustment. At last, a clear note floated through the dusty room. Grandfather looked up, smiling.
They hung the bell beside the workshop door. During the following week, Maya noticed that her grandfather rang it whenever he entered, even though it no longer announced a customer. On the day the shelves arrived, he handed her the shop’s faded wooden sign. “You understood that some things need patience, not replacement,” he said. “You should decide where this goes.”

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what directly creates a tone near a bridge edge?

choices.A: Steady changes in air pressure caused by repeating swirls
choices.B: Vehicles crossing narrow gaps at regular intervals
choices.C: Rainwater collecting inside hollow railings
choices.D: Cables striking one another in strong wind

questions.correctAnswer: Steady changes in air pressure caused by repeating swirls
questions.explanation: Repeating air swirls produce regular pressure changes that people hear as a tone.
questions.stimulusText:
On windy days, a bridge may produce a low hum, a whistle, or even a musical tone. These sounds do not necessarily indicate danger. They often begin when moving air interacts with railings, cables, or narrow gaps in the bridge’s structure.
As wind passes an edge, it can break into repeating swirls. Each swirl briefly changes the air pressure nearby. If those pressure changes occur at a steady rate, they create a vibration that people hear as a tone. The effect resembles the sound made by blowing across the opening of a bottle, although a bridge offers many more surfaces for the air to meet.
Engineers study these sounds because vibration matters even when a structure is safe. A persistent tone may disturb nearby residents, and repeated vibration can loosen small parts over time. Engineers may add thin barriers, alter the shape of a railing, or cover a gap so that air no longer forms regular swirls.
The goal is not always to silence the bridge completely. Wind changes direction and speed, so no single modification prevents every sound. Instead, engineers identify the surfaces producing the strongest vibrations and reduce those effects. Listening, therefore, becomes one of several tools for understanding how a bridge responds to its environment.

questions.skill: Main Idea, Central Thought, or Summary
questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

choices.A: Why beginning artists should avoid drawing crowded scenes
choices.B: How poster designers select words and pictures
choices.C: Why accurately drawing furniture requires geometry
choices.D: How empty areas contribute to observation and composition

questions.correctAnswer: How empty areas contribute to observation and composition
questions.explanation: The passage explains how negative space guides viewers, shapes mood, and helps artists observe proportions.
questions.stimulusText:
When people first study a drawing, they often concentrate on the objects: a vase, a face, or a row of buildings. Artists, however, also pay close attention to the unoccupied areas around and between those objects. This “negative space” is not simply a blank background. Its shape helps determine how the entire composition feels.
Consider a poster crowded with words and pictures. Even if every element is interesting, the viewer may not know where to look first. Empty areas can separate groups of information and guide the eye from a heading to an image and then to a smaller line of text. In a portrait, the open area beside a person’s face may create a sense of quiet, while a figure pressed close to every edge can seem confined.
Negative space also assists artists in observing accurately. Instead of trying to draw the complicated outline of a chair, a student might draw the triangular gaps between its legs. When those gaps have the correct proportions, the chair itself often becomes more accurate.
Paying attention to what is absent may feel unnatural at first. Yet this shift does not make the subject less important. It reveals that objects and their surroundings work together. A successful composition depends not only on what an artist includes, but also on the room each element is allowed to occupy.

questions.prompt: What did Nia do before choosing Juniper Lane as the detour?

choices.A: She tested the gravel path herself.
choices.B: She asked the riders to vote.
choices.C: She moved the safety meeting.
choices.D: She called the water crew.

questions.correctAnswer: She tested the gravel path herself.
questions.explanation: Nia rides the path to confirm that it is firm, wide, and safe before selecting it.
questions.stimulusText:
Nia had planned every turn of the neighborhood bicycle tour, but ten minutes before the riders arrived, orange barriers blocked Willow Street. A water crew had opened a trench across the road. Nia unfolded her map on a bench and stared at the neat blue line she had drawn the night before.
“We could cancel,” said Mr. Lee, the community-center director.
Nia shook her head. Several younger riders had practiced for weeks. She walked to the corner and studied the side streets. Juniper Lane curved toward the park, but she had never ridden its entire length. Just then, Mrs. Ortiz rolled up with a basket of library books on her bicycle. She explained that Juniper ended at a short gravel path before rejoining the planned route.
Nia tested the path herself. It was firm, wide, and free of traffic, though riders would need to walk their bicycles for fifty yards. She returned, marked the change, and explained it clearly at the safety meeting. During the tour, the group moved slowly over the gravel. The delay allowed them to notice a community garden hidden behind tall hedges. On the ride back, a child asked whether next month’s route could include the garden on purpose.
Nia smiled as she redrew the line on her map. The detour no longer looked like a mistake.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what is one effect of a maple seed’s rotation?

choices.A: It increases the seed’s mass.
choices.B: It causes the wing to grow longer.
choices.C: It returns the seed to the tree.
choices.D: It slows the seed’s downward motion.

questions.correctAnswer: It slows the seed’s downward motion.
questions.explanation: Autorotation produces an upward force that reduces the seed’s falling speed.
questions.stimulusText:
Some maple seeds travel through the air like tiny helicopters. Each seed is attached to a thin wing. When the seed falls, air pushes unevenly against the wing and begins turning it. This rotation, called autorotation, slows the seed’s downward motion.
The spinning wing creates differences in air pressure. Air moves faster over one part of the wing than another, producing an upward force. That force does not lift the seed back into the tree, but it reduces the speed of its fall. A slower descent gives wind more time to carry the seed away from the parent tree.
Researchers study this motion by dropping seed models in still air and recording them with high-speed cameras. They may change one feature at a time, such as wing length, seed mass, or the angle at which the wing bends. Comparing the recordings helps them determine how each feature affects rotation and falling speed.
This research has uses beyond explaining how trees spread. Engineers have tested small spinning devices that descend without motors or parachutes. Such devices might carry lightweight sensors through the air to measure temperature or air quality over a broad area. The maple seed offers a model: a simple shape can control motion by working with the surrounding air.

That force does not lift the seed back into the tree, but it reduces the speed of its fall. A slower descent gives wind more time to carry the seed away from the parent tree.
Researchers study this motion by dropping seed models in still air and recording them with high-speed cameras. They may change one feature at a time, such as wing length, seed mass, or the angle at which the wing bends. Comparing the recordings helps them determine how each feature affects rotation and falling speed.
This research has uses beyond explaining how trees spread. Engineers have tested small spinning devices that descend without motors or parachutes. Such devices might carry lightweight sensors through the air to measure temperature or air quality over a broad area. The maple seed offers a model: a simple shape can control motion by working with the surrounding air.

questions.stimulusText:
In many growing towns, street addresses were not always part of daily life. Residents might direct a visitor to “the blue house beyond the mill” or identify a shop by its owner’s name. Such descriptions worked when communities were small and landmarks were widely known.
As towns expanded, informal directions became less reliable. New residents did not recognize every family name, and several streets might contain similar buildings. Postal workers, firefighters, and delivery drivers needed a system that allowed them to locate a property without knowing its history.
Town officials began assigning names to streets and numbers to buildings. A useful numbering plan followed a predictable order. Often, odd numbers appeared on one side of a street and even numbers on the other. In some places, numbers increased with distance from a central road or town square. Signs at intersections made the system visible to people passing through.
Adopting addresses required more than attaching plaques to doors. Officials had to create accurate records, correct duplicate street names, and inform residents of changes. Despite the work involved, standardized addresses gradually became an important layer of public information. They helped strangers navigate a place by following shared rules rather than depending on local memory.

choices.A: She measured the space and checked the outlets.
choices.B: She painted a picture of the basement door.
choices.C: She moved the construction equipment.
choices.D: She invited Mr. Alvarez to perform.

questions.correctAnswer: She measured the space and checked the outlets.
questions.explanation: Lena measures the hallway and counts working outlets before requesting permission.
questions.stimulusText:
Each autumn, Lena’s apartment building held a lantern walk in the courtyard. Families carried glowing paper lanterns while Mr. Alvarez played old songs on his accordion. This year, however, the event nearly disappeared. The courtyard was being repaired, and the adults decided there was nowhere suitable to gather.
Lena disliked accepting that answer. In the basement, she noticed a long hallway leading past the storage rooms. It was plain and narrow, but it was also dry and free of construction equipment. She measured the hallway, counted the working outlets, and asked the superintendent whether the space could be used safely.
With permission, Lena invited neighbors to hang lanterns from removable hooks. Children painted paper panels with scenes from every floor of the building: Mrs. Chen’s window garden, the twins’ orange cat, and the rooftop water tank. Because an accordion would echo too loudly underground, Mr. Alvarez played softly near the entrance.
The walk was shorter than usual, yet people moved slowly, recognizing familiar details in the pictures. At the end of the hallway, Lena found one unpainted lantern. She added a picture of the basement door standing open. It was not the courtyard they remembered, but the narrow passage had become a map of the community above it.

questions.skill: Factual Comprehension, Detail, or Textual Evidence
questions.prompt: What caused the original rain gauge to lose water?

choices.A: The seal around a screw failed.
choices.B: The measurement marks washed away.
choices.C: The container tipped during the night.
choices.D: The tomato plants blocked the rain.

questions.correctAnswer: The seal around a screw failed.
questions.explanation: A water trail reveals that the faulty screw seal allowed rain to escape.
questions.stimulusText:
Owen had spent three weeks building a wooden rain gauge for the school garden. He sanded the post, marked a clear container in centimeters, and sealed every joint. On the morning of the science fair, he carried it outside and discovered that the container was empty, although rain had fallen all night.
His first thought was to hide the gauge behind the tomato plants. Then he noticed a thin trail of water running down the post. The seal around one screw had failed. Owen’s display board promised “accurate daily rainfall,” and visitors would arrive within an hour.
He found his teacher, Ms. Patel, and explained the leak. Together they placed a new container beside the faulty one. Owen added a card describing what had happened and invited visitors to predict whether the repair would work. Throughout the fair, students inspected the stain on the post and suggested ways to improve the seal.
Near closing time, a brief shower crossed the garden. The new container collected four millimeters of water. Owen was relieved, but he left the leaking gauge in place. His project had not produced the week of measurements he expected. Instead, it showed why scientists record problems rather than erase them. The empty container had become evidence too.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why might durable flooring be used near library entrances?

choices.A: It can withstand the rain and dirt brought inside.
choices.B: It absorbs more sound than ceiling tiles.
choices.C: It makes dropped books easier to hear.
choices.D: It directs visitors toward study areas.

questions.correctAnswer: It can withstand the rain and dirt brought inside.
questions.explanation: The passage directly states that entrance flooring may need durability because of rain and dirt.
questions.stimulusText:
Quiet rooms do not depend only on people whispering. Their design can also limit how sound travels. In a library, sound may bounce from hard floors, glass walls, and bare ceilings. These reflections allow a chair scraping in one corner to be heard far away.
Designers reduce reflected sound by including materials that absorb some of its energy. Carpet, fabric-covered panels, and certain ceiling tiles contain tiny spaces where vibrating air loses energy. Soft materials are not placed everywhere, however. Bookshelves already interrupt sound paths, and durable flooring may be necessary near entrances where rain and dirt are common.
The arrangement of rooms matters as well. Group-study areas can be separated from silent reading spaces by offices, stairways, or rows of shelving. Doors with tight seals prevent sound from escaping through gaps. Even the location of a return desk can make a difference because dropped books create brief, sharp noises.
No design can remove every sound, nor should it. People must communicate, alarms must be heard, and public spaces need to feel welcoming. Effective acoustic design therefore aims for balance. By controlling reflections and separating activities, a library can provide both lively places for cooperation and calmer places for concentration.

choices.D: A schedule posted by the building manager

questions.explanation: The note indicates that Mr. Ito is bringing supplies for the Tuesday group.
questions.stimulusText:
At the end of the community cooking workshop, Elena found a blue apron folded beneath a chair. A stitched silver fish marked one pocket. The other students had already left, and the building manager was stacking tables.
Elena could have placed the apron in the lost-and-found box, but the fish seemed familiar. During the workshop, Mr. Ito had demonstrated how to shape dumplings. He had worn a plain white apron, yet he had mentioned that his first job was at his aunt’s seafood café. Elena remembered seeing him carry two bags to his bicycle after class.
She hurried outside, but the bicycle rack was empty. Instead of guessing, Elena returned to the kitchen and examined the sign-in sheet. Beside Mr. Ito’s name was a note: “bringing supplies for Tuesday group.” Elena called the program office and learned that he would return the next afternoon.
On Tuesday, Mr. Ito smiled when Elena held up the apron. It belonged not to him but to his aunt, who had sewn the fish years ago. He had brought it to show the class and had not noticed it missing. Before leaving, he asked Elena to help him pin the apron beside an old café photograph for the next workshop. Elena had set out to return a forgotten object; now she understood why it had been worth identifying its owner carefully.

questions.stimulusText:
At the end of the community cooking workshop, Elena found a blue apron folded beneath a chair. A stitched silver fish marked one pocket. The other students had already left, and the building manager was stacking tables.
Elena could have placed the apron in the lost-and-found box, but the fish seemed familiar. During the workshop, Mr. Ito had demonstrated how to shape dumplings. He had worn a plain white apron, yet he had mentioned that his first job was at his aunt’s seafood café. Elena remembered seeing him carry two bags to his bicycle after class.
She hurried outside, but the bicycle rack was empty. Instead of guessing, Elena returned to the kitchen and examined the sign-in sheet. Beside Mr. Ito’s name was a note: “bringing supplies for Tuesday group.” Elena called the program office and learned that he would return the next afternoon.
On Tuesday, Mr. Ito smiled when Elena held up the apron. It belonged not to him but to his aunt, who had sewn the fish years ago. He had brought it to show the class and had not noticed it missing. Before leaving, he asked Elena to help him pin the apron beside an old café photograph for the next workshop. Elena had set out to return a forgotten object; now she understood why it had been worth identifying its owner carefully.

questions.stimulusTitle: A Cool Roof Above the Sidewalk
questions.stimulusText:
On a sunny day, a dark roof can absorb much of the sunlight that reaches it. The roof then releases some of that energy as heat, warming both the building and the nearby air. To reduce this effect, some buildings use “cool roofs,” which reflect more sunlight and release absorbed heat efficiently.
A cool roof is not necessarily bright white. Manufacturers can create lighter surfaces and specially coated materials in several colors. Researchers evaluate these products with instruments rather than judging by appearance alone. One measurement records solar reflectance, the fraction of incoming sunlight a surface sends away. Another records thermal emittance, the surface’s ability to release absorbed heat.
The benefits depend on location and building design. In a hot climate, a cooler roof may reduce the need for air-conditioning. A building shaded by tall trees, however, receives less direct sunlight, so changing its roof may have a smaller effect. Insulation, roof angle, local weather, and energy prices also influence the result.
City planners sometimes study groups of roofs because many hot surfaces close together can raise neighborhood temperatures. Cool roofs alone cannot solve urban heat, but they can work alongside shade trees, parks, and light-colored pavement. The most effective plan usually combines several methods selected for local conditions.

questions.correctAnswer: Common street names and notes about access
questions.explanation: The passage states that Bell’s separate guide recorded local names and access information.
questions.stimulusText:
When surveyor Amara Bell arrived in the growing river town of Northbank in 1912, officials gave her a straightforward assignment: prepare a dependable street map. Existing maps showed major roads, but several lanes had changed names, and new workshops crowded the waterfront.
Bell began with instruments, measuring distances and recording angles. She soon discovered, however, that measurements could not explain every route. A narrow passage appeared to end at a fence, yet workers told her that a gate opened during market hours. A road marked “Mill Lane” was called “Dock Road” by delivery drivers. Bell therefore added interviews to her fieldwork. She asked residents how streets were used, when gates opened, and which landmarks helped visitors.
Her completed map included official names, but a separate guide recorded common local names and access notes. Some officials initially objected that these details made the project less tidy. Bell replied that a useful map should describe movement, not merely lines. After emergency crews used her access notes to reach a waterfront fire quickly, the guide became part of the town’s standard records.
Bell’s work illustrates a lasting principle of mapmaking: accuracy includes human experience. Measurements establish location, while observation and local knowledge reveal how places function. Neither source is sufficient by itself.
